clips.title: Introducing repository rules
clips.why: GitHub's own two-minute introduction to rulesets, the feature we switch on for fcp's main.
look: Rulesets are named sets of rules that can be layered, instead of one branch protection setting per branch.
The part on guardrails versus empowerment: rules should stop real mistakes without slowing honest work, which is the point of the dry run.
The evaluate mode it mentions: a way to see what a rule would block before it blocks anything.
clips.after: fcp already has a disabled ruleset for main; our job is to make it passable for every honest pull request and then set it to active.

clips.title: Conditional branch protection for monorepos on Github using GHA
clips.why: He hits our exact problem in his own monorepo: tests that should only run when a folder changes, and a branch rule that requires them anyway.
look: The moment the folder filter and the required check collide: a pull request that changed other folders waits for a check that never comes.
How his path filters decide which tests run, and where in the workflow that decision is made.
Compare his fix with ours, a job that starts, skips itself and still reports.
clips.after: fcp's check-changes job is the same idea: the workflow always starts, and the unit-test job skips itself when its area did not change.

clips.title: Break Glass Accounts   What are They
clips.why: Break-glass accounts come from identity security, and the same rules apply to our emergency door on main.
look: How few people should hold the emergency power, and why two is a good number.
Why every use must raise an alert that someone actually reads.
That the emergency path should be tested before the emergency, not during it.
clips.after: Our door is the fcp-break-glass team: two leads, bypass only through a pull request, every bypass logged and read in the weekly review.

practice.q: The ruleset requires Frontend Unit Tests. A backend-only pull request runs frontend-ci.yaml, whose unit-test job has if: needs.check-changes.outputs.frontend == 'true'. What does the pull request show for Frontend Unit Tests?

options.text: Nothing: the check never appears, and the pull request waits.
options.why: That is what a paths: filter does. Here the workflow starts, so the job reports.

options.text: skipped, which the required check accepts as passing.
options.why: The job started, its if: was false, so it reports skipped. Skipped satisfies a required check.

options.text: failure, because the condition was false.
options.why: A false if: condition skips a job; it never marks it as failed.

practice.q: Finish the job so that the name matches the ruleset's required check exactly.
practice.hint: The ruleset lists Cloud, Client and ... Unit Tests.
practice.why: A required check is found by the job's name, letter for letter. Three jobs named Unit Tests cannot be told apart.

practice.q: Put the steps of switching on main's ruleset in order.
items: The engineering leads agree the review rules, the requester and break-glass, and the page is written
The three unit-test jobs get distinct names and lose their paths: filters
A dry run of today's open pull requests shows none that could never merge
An org admin sets the ruleset to active with the agreed rules
A test pull request without approval cannot merge, and a frontend-only one merges after one approval
The ruleset is exported as JSON next to the rules page
practice.why: People first, then make the wall passable, then switch it on, then test it and keep the record.

practice.q: The CI fixer, a routine owned by Lior, opens a pull request to fix red main. Lior approves it, and nobody else does. Can it merge?

options.text: Yes, Lior is an engineer and one approval is required.
options.why: For a routine, the owner is the requester. The requester's approval never counts.

options.text: No. Lior is the requester of the routine's pull request, so someone else must approve.
options.why: The rules name the routine's owner as the requester, and the independent-approval check enforces it.

options.text: No, routine pull requests need two approvals.
options.why: Every pull request needs exactly one approval. What matters is who gives it.

practice.q: Who is on fcp main's bypass list?

options.text: Every org admin, because admins are exempt from rulesets.
options.why: Admins are not exempt. Only the listed bypass actors are.

options.text: The break-glass team of two leads, and only through a pull request.
options.why: One team, bypass_mode pull_request, every bypass logged and read weekly.

options.text: The break-glass team and the agents' GitHub App, so fixes can land fast.
options.why: Agents never merge, so the App is never a bypass actor.
